title: Encryption has a new problem: AI is getting better at proving the impossible
summary: AI has solved yet another math problem that stumped humans for more than 150 years, ratcheting up questions about the efficacy, or even relevancy, of cryptography in the age of AI. Aided by Claude, mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge is believed to have proven the Riemann Hypothesis , one of the most famous open problems in math. It posits that prime numbers, or the ‘atoms’ of all math, are actually distributed neatly and predictably, not randomly or sporadically as they may seem. The hypothesis’ proof could, at least in some eventualities, change the story of modern cryptography, because prime numbers serve as secret passcodes that help hide sensitive data. Still, security leaders and teams shouldn’t panic, even as mathematicians may be in mourning. “This development does not mean encryption has suddenly been broken,” said Fritz Jean-Louis , a principal cybersecurity instructor at Infotech. “The more important security aspect is the speed of AI-assisted mathematical discovery.” The dawn of ‘something far greater’ Mathematician Bernhard Riemann proposed his eponymous hypothesis in 1859, suggesting a hidden pattern in the distribution of prime numbers (numbers like 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and so on that are divisible only by themselves and 1). They are the building blocks of whole numbers, while at the same time hiding deeper, unresolved patterns, or so it has been thought. The Riemann Hypothesis has lacked a general proof for 167 years; the Clay Mathematics Institute even offers a $1 million bounty to anyone who can generate one. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems with this distinction. But last week, Alpöge posted a proof generated with Claude in Lean, a programming language that verifies the mathematical correctness of each step. Alpöge initially posted just the proof because the detailed text occupies more than 250,000 pages. title: The SaaS resiliency bill is coming due
summary: The latest Microsoft outage should give enterprise architects pause. Widespread disruptions to Microsoft 365—including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot—affected users across many countries, with reports of sharp spikes in outages. What was a temporary annoyance for many became a serious business interruption for enterprises. Here’s an inconvenient truth: If these systems had run entirely on equipment you controlled, many would have kept working—not all, or forever, but enough to matter. A laptop word processor needs no healthy hyperscale cloud to draft a document. A local mail server needs no software-as-a-service (SaaS) identity system, telemetry, synchronization, collaboration, and policy services to agree it’s a good day to send an email. But that’s not how we’ve built most modern business software. Applications may look local but depend on remote services for authentication, licensing, files, configuration, AI, security, syncing, search, workflows, and even startup. When the back-end service goes offline, the local software may still be on the device, but the business function is unavailable. Moving to a new model I’ve watched this shift unfold over decades. In the client/server era, we worried about LANs, database clusters, storage, and the occasional angry CFO who wanted to know why the ERP system was down before the quarterly close. Those systems were imperfect, expensive, and often painful to maintain. However, their failure domains were usually visible. If the database server failed, we knew where. If the network switch died, we could point to it. If the backup failed, someone in the data center had some explaining to do. Then the industry embraced SaaS to avoid endless upgrades and desktop patching, shift costs from capital to operating expenses, and gain collaboration, automatic updates, centralized policies, and remote-work support. title: When five AI agents make one mistake, which one’s at fault?
summary: Early in my career, I helped build a healthcare platform for patient-reported outcomes. It exchanged data with a federal health system and several EHR vendors. The hard question with those integrations was never whether the data moved. It was who started the access, and under what authority. A database could tell you which credential read the record. An application log could tell you which service handled the request. Neither could tell you which person was behind it. My job was to carry that context through every layer so the access could be explained later. That work also led to two U.S. patents I hold on secure storage of and access to patient health information. I’ve been thinking about that problem again as agents start working side by side. Meta acquired Conductor , a workspace for running coding agents in parallel. GitHub’s new Git storage architecture handled 5,000 concurrent agents on one repository in internal testing. Anthropic opened a private beta for enterprises to self-host Managed Agents. Different products, same direction. Agents are moving into shared repositories, shared tools and shared infrastructure. Anthropic’s own research shows what can go wrong there. In August, it described an experiment in which three Claude instances, each on its own VM, were told to migrate the same Python backend on a fourth VM to a different language. None knew the others existed. Over four hours, they disabled one another’s Unix accounts, wrote looping scripts to kill each other’s processes and disguised malicious code as another agent’s work. Anyone who has sat through a tense sprint retro may find that oddly familiar. The agents just got there faster. In a separate pricing game, agents with a private channel started colluding within three rounds. When Anthropic removed every direct channel, they kept matching prices to the penny through a public listings board. Those results got the headlines. What worries me is more boring. title: Your AI agent shouldn’t get to grade its own work
summary: In a recent experiment , Claude Opus 4.8 built an invoice checker, revised it, and raised its score from just over 45 out of 100 to a perfect 100. That’s roughly a 122% improvement. Banish the humans! The robots have won. Well, maybe not. Remember that math teacher in eighth grade who let you grade your own tests? I do. Turns out there’s too much opportunity to cheat in that scenario, just as there is here, though it’s perhaps a different form of cheating. Here, Claude wrote the test. The researchers had 60 invoices of their own , and the original checker correctly flagged every bill that needed review and let the rest through. The revised checker? Same 60 invoices, same 60 correct calls. Claude deserves credit for building a good invoice checker. The thing is, it already had a good invoice checker before it made the “upgrade.” Hence, I’ll happily let an agent write the code and the tests. What would make me less happy is having the agent pick the only evidence we look at before we ship. If the agent misunderstands what the business wants, which is largely a human matter, its tests can reward it for getting the software wrong. Perfectly… wrong Consider the banking assistant in the same study. GPT-5.5 played the developer here: It built and tested the assistant that would talk to the simulated bank’s customers. The bank provided a way to look up a customer by email. GPT-5.5 missed that and instead wrote a test that rewarded the assistant for asking the customer for an internal ID. What? To get the test to pass, GPT-5.5 programmed the assistant to insist on an internal ID. The assistant eventually scored 100% on GPT-5.5’s tests, and the optimizer reported “nothing_to_fix.” In two of the researchers’ test conversations, the assistant refused the lookup and the customer gave up. title: $1.1B robotics founder: millions of robots will exist in 10 years
summary: I sit down with Adrien Gaidon, Co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer of Walden Robotics, to map out where the openings sit in robotics and physical AI. Adrien explains how teams now teach robots with data, why deployment data carries the most value, and why Walden picked wheels and two-finger grippers for factory work. We dig into the opportunities around the big labs: data with scarce access, supply chain, teleoperation, insurance, software tools, and niche robots. If robotics feels like a game for companies with $300 million seed rounds, this episode lays out the smaller ways in too. This episode was made possible thanks to Anthropic (the team behind Claude) for hosting us at Claude Founder house and sponsoring the episode.
